# Introduction

Beyond equilibrium phase structure, Rydberg atom arrays are a premier platform for studying non-equilibrium quantum dynamics.
The combination of strong blockade constraints, programmable geometry, global coherent driving, and site-resolved readout gives direct experimental access to phenomena that are theoretically rich and classically hard to simulate: anomalous thermalization from quantum many-body scars, discrete time-translation symmetry breaking, quantum coarsening after a phase transition, and information scrambling.

This page covers:

- PXP Hamiltonian and quantum many-body scars (QMBS)
- Floquet stabilization of scars and discrete time crystals (DTCs)
- Higher-order $n$-DTCs via EIT driving
- Quantum coarsening and the amplitude (Higgs) mode
- Out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) and information scrambling
- Emergent disorder from atomic position noise


# PXP Hamiltonian and quantum many-body scars {#sec-pxp}

## Hamiltonian and constrained Hilbert space

The PXP model is the strong-blockade ($V_{ij} \gg \Omega$ for nearest neighbors) limit of the Rydberg Hamiltonian.
Projecting out all configurations with adjacent Rydberg excitations yields the constrained Hamiltonian
$$
H_{\text{PXP}} = \frac{\Omega}{2}\sum_i P_{i-1}\,\sigma^x_i\, P_{i+1}
$$ {#eq-pxp}
where $P_i = |g_i\rangle\langle g_i|$ enforces the blockade constraint on both neighbors.
The Hilbert space dimension grows as $\sim \varphi^N$ (golden ratio $\varphi = (1+\sqrt{5})/2$) rather than $2^N$, corresponding to the Fibonacci constraint: no two adjacent sites can be simultaneously excited.

Despite the constraint, the PXP model is **non-integrable** — its level statistics follow the Wigner–Dyson distribution expected of a thermalizing (GOE) system.

## Scar tower and anomalous revivals

:::{#thm-scar-revivals .callout-important icon="false"}
## (Anomalous revivals from the Néel state)
The PXP Hamiltonian (@eq-pxp) on a 1D chain contains a set of anomalous eigenstates — **quantum many-body scars** — approximately equally spaced in energy by $\Delta E \approx 1.33\,\Omega$.
The Néel state $|Z_2\rangle = |rgrg\cdots\rangle$ has high overlap with these scar eigenstates, producing coherent revivals of the fidelity $|\langle Z_2 | e^{-iHt} | Z_2 \rangle|^2$ with period $T \approx 2\pi/\Delta E$, while generic initial states thermalize rapidly [@bernien2017probing; @turner2018weak].
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof sketch
The scar eigenstates can be understood via a forward-scattering approximation (FSA): starting from $|Z_2\rangle$, repeatedly applying $H_{\text{PXP}}$ generates a Krylov subspace of dimension $\sim N/2$.
The tridiagonal matrix of $H_{\text{PXP}}$ restricted to this subspace has approximately equally spaced eigenvalues, producing the quasi-periodic revivals.
The FSA eigenstates have anomalously low entanglement entropy ($S \sim \log N$ vs.\ the volume-law $S \sim N$ of thermal eigenstates at the same energy density), violating the strong eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH).
See [@turner2018weak; @serbyn2021quantum] for detailed analysis.
$\square$
:::

The scar tower is **not exact** — the revivals decay over $\sim 5$–$10$ oscillation periods due to leakage into the thermal bulk.
Approximate analytic forms for the scar eigenstates have been constructed using the AKLT formalism and spectrum-generating algebras, but a complete closed-form description of PXP scars remains an open problem [@serbyn2021quantum].


# Discrete time crystals {#sec-dtc}

## Floquet-stabilized scars

Periodic driving can be used to stabilize scar revivals and induce discrete time-translation symmetry breaking.

:::{#thm-dtc .callout-important icon="false"}
## (Scar-stabilized DTC)
Consider the Floquet protocol on a PXP chain: alternating periods of free PXP evolution and a global $\pi$-pulse $\prod_i \sigma^x_i$ with period $T$.
When the scar revival period is commensurate with $T$, the system exhibits **subharmonic response** at frequency $\omega/2$ (period $2T$), breaking the discrete time-translation symmetry of the drive.
This constitutes a discrete time crystal (DTC) stabilized by the scar subspace rather than by disorder-induced many-body localization [@bluvstein2021controlling; @else2016floquet].
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof sketch
In the standard DTC paradigm [@else2016floquet], many-body localization (MBL) protects the subharmonic response from heating.
The scar-stabilized mechanism is different: the non-thermal scar eigenstates act as an effective "noiseless subspace" within the Floquet spectrum.
The Néel state, having high overlap with scars, exhibits period-doubled dynamics because the scar quasi-energies are approximately $\pi/T$-spaced in the Floquet zone.
Perturbations away from the ideal $\pi$-pulse are absorbed by the rigidity of the scar spacing.
The key experimental signature is that the DTC response persists for the scar initial state ($|Z_2\rangle$) but not for generic (e.g., polarized $|gg\cdots g\rangle$) initial states.
See [@bluvstein2021controlling] for the Floquet analysis.
$\square$
:::

[@bluvstein2021controlling] demonstrated this on a 1D array of $\sim 25$ $^{87}$Rb atoms, observing period-doubled oscillations of the staggered magnetization persisting over ${\sim}100$ Floquet cycles.
They confirmed the scar mechanism by showing that the DTC signal is present for $|Z_2\rangle$ but absent for non-scar initial states.


## Higher-order $n$-DTCs {#sec-ndtc}

The Rydberg platform is not limited to period-2 DTCs.
[@kongkhambut2024higher] demonstrated higher-order and fractional DTCs with cesium atoms using an electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) scheme.
The three-level $|g\rangle \to |e\rangle \to |r\rangle$ ladder provides an additional control knob — the intermediate-state detuning — that tunes the effective interaction range and Floquet dynamics.

By applying pulsed RF driving with period $T$, they observed subharmonic response at periods $nT$ for integer $n$ up to $n = 14$, as well as fractional responses (e.g., $3T/2$).
The hierarchy of $n$-DTCs arises from parametric resonances in the driven interacting EIT system.
The experiment was performed in an ensemble geometry (not a tweezer array), with long-range dipolar interactions between Rydberg-dressed atoms providing the many-body coupling.


# Quantum coarsening and Higgs mode {#sec-coarsening}

## Coarsening dynamics after crossing the QPT

When a Rydberg array prepared in a paramagnetic (disordered) state is quenched across the $Z_2$ quantum phase transition into the antiferromagnetically ordered phase, the system initially forms a mosaic of $|Z_2\rangle$ and $|\bar{Z}_2\rangle$ domains separated by domain walls.
The subsequent dynamics is **quantum coarsening**: domains grow as domain-wall pairs annihilate, driven by the curvature of domain boundaries.

:::{#thm-coarsening .callout-important icon="false"}
## (Curvature-driven quantum coarsening)
On a 2D Rydberg array quenched into the $Z_2$ ordered phase, the characteristic domain size $\ell(t)$ grows as a power law $\ell(t) \sim t^\alpha$ at early-to-intermediate times.
Near the quantum critical point, coarsening is accelerated ($\alpha$ increases), and the dynamics is accompanied by long-lived oscillations of the order parameter at a frequency set by the amplitude (Higgs) mode of the ordered phase [@bluvstein2025quantum].
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof sketch
In the classical Allen–Cahn theory, domains with curvature $\kappa$ shrink at rate $\dot{R} \propto -\kappa$, yielding $\ell(t) \sim t^{1/2}$.
The quantum setting modifies this through coherent domain-wall dynamics and the proximity to the QPT, where the order-parameter gap (Higgs mass) softens.
The oscillation frequency of the staggered magnetization matches the Higgs mode $\omega_H \propto |\Delta - \Delta_c|^{z\nu}$, confirming its identity as the amplitude mode of the $Z_2$ order parameter.
See [@bluvstein2025quantum] for the full experimental and numerical analysis.
$\square$
:::


## Amplitude (Higgs) mode

The **Higgs mode** is the massive amplitude fluctuation of the order parameter in a broken-symmetry phase — the condensed-matter analog of the Higgs boson.
In the Rydberg $Z_2$ ordered phase, it corresponds to oscillations in the magnitude of the staggered magnetization at fixed phase (i.e., the system oscillates between stronger and weaker $Z_2$ order without switching between $|Z_2\rangle$ and $|\bar{Z}_2\rangle$).

[@bluvstein2025quantum] observed the Higgs mode on a $\sim 200$-atom 2D square-lattice array.
After a slow ramp across the QPT, the staggered magnetization exhibited damped oscillations superimposed on the coarsening growth.
The oscillation frequency decreased as $\Delta \to \Delta_c$ from the ordered side, consistent with the expected softening of the Higgs mass at criticality.
This constitutes the first observation of a quantum Higgs mode in a programmable quantum simulator.


# Information scrambling and OTOCs {#sec-otoc}

## Out-of-time-ordered correlators in Rydberg chains

The out-of-time-ordered correlator (OTOC)
$$
F(i, j, t) = \langle W_i^\dagger(t)\, V_j^\dagger\, W_i(t)\, V_j \rangle
$$ {#eq-otoc}
quantifies the spread of quantum information: $1 - |F|$ grows as the initially local operator $W_i(t) = e^{iHt} W_i e^{-iHt}$ develops support on site $j$.
In chaotic systems, the OTOC decays monotonically with a ballistic light-cone front.

The PXP model, with its coexistence of thermal and scar eigenstates, produces distinctive OTOC dynamics.

## Collapse-and-revival of OTOCs

[@chen2024collapse] measured OTOCs in a Rydberg atom array (Lin Li group, HUST) by implementing a time-reversal protocol: evolve forward under $H_{\text{PXP}}$, apply a local perturbation, evolve backward, and measure the overlap.
Starting from $|Z_2\rangle$, they observed **collapse-and-revival** patterns in the OTOC rather than the monotonic decay expected for a fully thermalizing system.
The revival period matches the scar oscillation period, confirming that the scar subspace imprints its coherent dynamics onto the information spreading.

## Anomalous scrambling from scar-induced periodicity

[@zhang2025anomalous] extended the OTOC measurements to extract the butterfly velocity $v_B$ and Lyapunov-like growth rate.
They found **anomalous scrambling**: the OTOC light cone exhibits periodic modulation with the scar revival period, leading to a time-dependent effective butterfly velocity.
This contrasts sharply with both integrable systems (no scrambling) and generic chaotic systems (monotonic ballistic scrambling), placing PXP in a distinct dynamical universality class.


# Emergent disorder from position noise {#sec-disorder}

Real Rydberg tweezer arrays have finite atomic position uncertainty $\delta r$ (typically $\delta r/a \sim 0.01$–$0.05$ from residual thermal motion in the tweezer).
Because the van der Waals interaction scales as $1/r^6$, even small position fluctuations produce significant disorder in the effective coupling constants:
$$
\delta V_{ij}/V_{ij} \approx 6\,\delta r/R_{ij}.
$$

[@maskara2025emergent] studied this effect on the 256-atom QuEra Aquila processor.
They found that atomic position noise acts as **emergent quenched disorder** in the effective Hamiltonian, even though the atoms are loaded deterministically.
Key consequences include:

- **Sub-ballistic entanglement growth**: the entanglement entropy grows as $S(t) \sim t^\beta$ with $\beta < 1$, slower than the ballistic $\beta = 1$ expected for a clean system.
- **Suppressed scar revivals**: the position-noise-induced disorder competes with the scar mechanism, reducing revival fidelity. The decay rate of revivals is quantitatively predicted by the variance of interaction energies.
- **Modified correlation spreading**: the light cone of connected correlations $\langle n_i(t) n_j(0) \rangle_c$ develops a sub-ballistic front, consistent with a crossover toward many-body localization physics at strong disorder.

This work highlights that emergent disorder is a fundamental consideration for large-scale analog quantum simulation, particularly near quantum critical points where the system is most sensitive to perturbations.


# Experiment overview {#sec-experiments}

## Lukin group (Harvard / QuEra)

**1. Bernien et al. (2017)** [@bernien2017probing] — *51 atoms, 1D chain.* First observation of anomalous revivals from $|Z_2\rangle$ in the blockade regime. The unexpected persistent oscillations — later identified as QMBS — launched the field.

**2. Bluvstein et al. (2021)** [@bluvstein2021controlling] — *$\sim$25 atoms, 1D chain.* Demonstrated Floquet control of scar dynamics: stabilization, enhancement, and inversion of revivals via periodic driving. First scar-stabilized DTC with subharmonic ($2T$) response.

**3. Bluvstein et al. (2025)** [@bluvstein2025quantum] — *$\sim$200 atoms, 2D square lattice.* Observed quantum coarsening of $Z_2$ domains after crossing the Ising QPT. Identified the amplitude (Higgs) mode from damped oscillations of the order parameter. First quantum Higgs mode in a programmable simulator.

**4. Maskara et al. (2025)** [@maskara2025emergent] — *256 atoms, 1D and 2D arrays (QuEra Aquila).* Showed that atomic position noise produces emergent quenched disorder, causing sub-ballistic entanglement growth and suppressed scar revivals.


## Lin Li group (HUST)

**5. Chen et al. (2024)** [@chen2024collapse] — *$\sim$20 atoms, 1D chain.* Measured OTOCs in a Rydberg PXP system via time-reversal protocol. Observed collapse-and-revival of quantum information, with revival period matching scar oscillations.

**6. Zhang et al. (2025)** [@zhang2025anomalous] — *$\sim$20 atoms, 1D chain.* Extracted butterfly velocity and scrambling rate from OTOC measurements. Found anomalous periodically-modulated scrambling characteristic of scar-induced non-ergodicity.


## Kongkhambut et al. (Hamburg)

**7. Kongkhambut et al. (2024)** [@kongkhambut2024higher] — *Cs ensemble, EIT scheme.* Demonstrated higher-order DTCs with subharmonic response at periods up to $n = 14$ times the drive period, as well as fractional DTCs, using pulsed RF driving of Rydberg-dressed cesium atoms.

# Open problems {#sec-open}

1. **Scar structure in 2D.** The PXP scar tower is well-characterized in 1D chains. Whether analogous scar towers exist in 2D blockade-constrained systems (e.g., on the square or triangular lattice) — and whether they can be experimentally detected — is largely unexplored.

2. **Engineered scar subspaces.** Can one programmably design scar Hamiltonians to protect targeted quantum states from thermalization? This would connect QMBS to quantum error correction and autonomous quantum memories.

3. **DTC thermodynamic stability.** The scar-stabilized DTC eventually decays due to leakage into the thermal bulk. The asymptotic lifetime scaling with system size — and whether a true thermodynamic DTC phase exists without MBL — remains an open theoretical question.

4. **Universal coarsening exponents.** The coarsening exponent $\alpha$ and its dependence on dimensionality, universality class, and proximity to the QPT have not been precisely measured. Comparison to the classical Allen–Cahn prediction ($\alpha = 1/2$) in the quantum regime is outstanding.

5. **OTOC quantitative benchmarks.** Current OTOC measurements are on $\sim 20$-atom systems. Scaling to larger arrays would enable extraction of the scrambling exponent and definitive comparison between scar-dominated and thermal scrambling regimes.

6. **Position noise mitigation.** The emergent-disorder results of [@maskara2025emergent] imply that position-noise control is a bottleneck for large-scale analog simulation fidelity. Quantifying the noise threshold for reliable quantum simulation near criticality — and developing cooling or feedback protocols to suppress it — is a pressing engineering challenge.
